items.text: All 4 round-1 decisions are settled: DM owns the release record (d1→A), UUID as canonical ID (d2→B), channel promotion defined now (d3→A), release notes on the record (d4→A). The conclusion now includes a concrete SQL schema for `releases` and `release_platforms` tables, Go type definitions, channel ordering model (nightly→beta→stable), and 6 implementation actions.

DM's `deployments` table currently has no `git_commit_hash` column — it only stores status, timestamps, message, logs, and a JSONB `artifacts` field. The release record effectively replaces deployments as the audit trail for 'what was published.' The existing deployments table can continue to track execution mechanics (logs, errors) while the releases table tracks the semantic release event.

S2D's 4-step LPBS upload (presign→S3→commit→apply) already passes `release_version` and `git_commit_hash` in the commit step. Adding `release_id` requires only a new field on `UploadRequest` and inclusion in the commit HTTP body — no structural changes to the upload flow.

LPBS's `UpsertAsset` currently hardcodes `variant_key = 'default'` (download_service.go line 596). For multi-channel releases, this must become a parameter so S2D can pass the target channel's variant_key. This is a small but critical change that falls out of the channel model decision.

items.topic: Should the release record link to a deployment or replace the deployment as the top-level entity?
items.context: DM currently creates a `deployments` row to track each pipeline execution (status, logs, artifacts JSONB). The new `releases` table tracks the semantic release event (version, channel, approval, per-platform status). These overlap: both track 'did we successfully publish?' Options affect whether existing deployment code needs refactoring.

options.label: releases references deployments — add deployment_id FK on releases
options.rationale: Keeps both tables. A release is triggered by a deployment. Deployment holds execution details (logs, timing), release holds semantic details (version, channel, status). Clean separation of concerns but two tables to query for full picture.

options.label: releases replaces deployments — migrate execution fields into releases
options.rationale: Single table for everything. Simpler queries. But the releases table becomes very wide, and non-release deployments (like dry runs or validation-only runs) would need to fit the schema.

options.label: releases and deployments stay independent — correlate only via git_commit_hash
options.rationale: No schema coupling between the two. Each table serves its purpose independently. Correlation is possible via commit hash but not enforced. Simplest migration path.

items.topic: How should multi-platform releases be modeled: one release spans all platforms, or one release per platform?
items.context: The proposed schema has one `releases` row per (profile, commit, channel) with child `release_platforms` rows per platform. This means a single release can be partially published (e.g., Windows published, Mac still building). An alternative is one release per (profile, commit, channel, platform), which is simpler but loses the concept of a cohesive cross-platform release.

options.label: One release, multiple platforms (parent-child as proposed)
options.rationale: Matches the real-world concept: 'v1.2.3 for stable' is one release that happens to have multiple platform builds. Enables 'is the full release done?' queries. Allows partial publication tracking. This is the schema in the current conclusion.

options.label: One release per platform — flatten into a single table
options.rationale: Simpler schema (no join needed). Each row is fully self-contained. But 'list all releases' returns 3 rows per version (one per platform), and there's no natural way to ask 'is release X fully published across all platforms?'

items.topic: When should nightly channel releases skip approval gates?
items.context: The channel model defines nightly as 'no approval required.' But DM's existing `CheckReleaseGate()` enforces approval for all platforms. We need to decide how the gate interacts with channels. This affects the `release_platforms.approval_id` field — for nightly releases it would be NULL.

options.label: Channel-based gate bypass: nightly skips approval, beta requires approval, stable requires all-platform approval
options.rationale: Clean tiered model. Nightly is fully automated (CI-triggered). Beta needs at least one reviewer. Stable uses the existing full gate. Maps naturally to the ChannelOrder.

options.label: Per-profile gate configuration: each profile defines which channels require approval
options.rationale: More flexible — some profiles might want nightly gating too. But adds configuration complexity and a new table or JSONB field on profiles.

options.label: No gate bypass — all channels require approval, but nightly auto-approves
options.rationale: Uniform model (every release has an approval record). Nightly approval is system-generated. Audit trail is complete but noisy.

items.text: The `promoted_from_release_id` chain enables full promotion traceability: given any stable release, you can walk back to see it was promoted from beta, which was promoted from nightly, which was the original build. This supports audit questions like 'how long was v1.2.3 in beta before going stable?' via simple timestamp comparison on the chain.

Created 6 concrete implementation actions. Methodology expanded with round 2 deep-dive details.
